subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Share a Pizza
hook: Learn fractions by sharing pizza and sweets with Arjun and Priya!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A pizza-loving 12-year-old learning to share fairly

slides.title: Arjun and Priya Share a Pizza
A Pizza Divided
slides.storyContext: At a cafe, Arjun and Priya order a pizza cut into 8 equal slices. Arjun takes 3 slices. That's 3/8 of the pizza, says Priya. The top number tells us how many parts we have. The bottom number tells us how many equal parts the whole pizza is cut into.
slides.inSimpleWords: A fraction shows a part of a whole.

image.alt: A Pizza Divided — Working with Fractions

slides.title: What Is a Fraction?
slides.storyContext: Priya explains to Arjun: A fraction is a way to show a part of a whole thing. If we divide something into equal pieces and take some, we use fractions to describe it.

points.label: Fractions Show Parts
points.text: A fraction = part ÷ whole. If a pizza has 8 slices and you take 3, you have 3/8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions tell us what part of something we have.

slides.title: Numerator and Denominator
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: In 3/8, the 3 is the numerator - the number on top, showing how many parts we have. The 8 is the denominator - the number on bottom, showing the total parts. She draws a pizza diagram. If we have 3/8, we're missing 5/8. Together: 3/8 + 5/8 = 8/8 = 1 whole pizza!

points.label: Parts of a Fraction
points.text: Numerator (top): parts we have. Denominator (bottom): total parts the whole is divided into.

example.solution: 5 = parts we have. 12 = total parts in the whole

slides.inSimpleWords: Top number = parts we have. Bottom number = total parts.

image.alt: Numerator and Denominator — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Comparing Fractions — Which Piece Is Bigger?
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya each get a pastry. Arjun eats 1/2. Priya eats 1/4. Who ate more? asks Arjun. Priya draws two rectangles: one divided into 2 parts with 1 shaded, another into 4 parts with 1 shaded. 1/2 is bigger! If the denominator is smaller, the pieces are bigger.

points.label: Comparing Fractions
points.text: Same numerator: smaller denominator = bigger fraction. 1/2 > 1/4. Same denominator: bigger numerator = bigger fraction. 3/8 > 2/8.

example.solution: 2/5. Same numerator, so the one with smaller denominator is bigger.

slides.inSimpleWords: To compare fractions, look at numerators and denominators.

slides.title: Adding Fractions (Same Denominator)
slides.storyContext: Priya has 2/8 of a barfi. Arjun has 3/8. Let's combine them! says Priya. 2/8 + 3/8: we just add the top numbers and keep the bottom. 2 + 3 = 5, so we get 5/8.

points.label: Adding Fractions
points.text: If denominators are the same, add numerators: a/c + b/c = (a+b)/c

slides.inSimpleWords: Add fractions by adding tops if bottoms match.

image.alt: Adding Fractions (Same Denominator) — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Worked Example: Adding Same Denominators
slides.storyContext: Let's practice! Priya says: Add 3/10 + 4/10. The denominators match, so we add the numerators: 3 + 4 = 7. Answer: 7/10. Arjun tries: 2/7 + 3/7 = (2+3)/7 = 5/7. Easy!

points.label: Step-by-Step
points.text: 1. Check denominators match. 2. Add numerators. 3. Keep denominator. 4. Write answer.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add the tops, keep the bottoms same.

slides.title: Finding Common Denominators
slides.storyContext: Arjun has 1/2 of a gulab jamun. Priya has 1/3. Can we add these? asks Arjun. Priya thinks. 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6. Now they have the same bottom! 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6! Arjun's eyes light up. We found a common denominator!

points.label: Common Denominators
points.text: Rewrite fractions so they have the same denominator. Find the LCM of the denominators.

slides.inSimpleWords: Make bottoms the same before adding fractions.

image.alt: Finding Common Denominators — Working with Fractions

slides.title: How to Find a Common Denominator
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches the method: To add 1/3 + 1/5, find a number both 3 and 5 divide into evenly. The LCM of 3 and 5 is 15. Convert: 1/3 = 5/15 and 1/5 = 3/15. Now add: 5/15 + 3/15 = 8/15!

points.label: Converting to Common Denominators
points.text: Find LCM of denominators. Multiply each fraction by the same factor to reach that LCM.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply both parts of a fraction by the same number.

slides.title: Multiplying Fractions
slides.storyContext: Arjun says: What's 1/2 of 2/3 of a chocolate bar? Priya multiplies: 1/2 x 2/3: multiply tops and bottoms. (1x2)/(2x3) = 2/6 = 1/3. She shades a bar to show. Yes, exactly 1/3 of a bar!

points.label: Multiplying Fractions
points.text: (a/b) x (c/d) = (a×c)/(b×d). Multiply tops and bottoms.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply fractions by multiplying tops and bottoms.

image.alt: Multiplying Fractions — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Subtracting Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya has 5/8 of a samosa. She eats 2/8. How much is left? 5/8 - 2/8 = (5-2)/8 = 3/8. Subtraction works like addition: if the bottoms are the same, just subtract the tops!

points.label: Subtracting Fractions
points.text: Same denominator: subtract numerators. a/c - b/c = (a-b)/c

slides.inSimpleWords: Subtract fractions like you add them.

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya draws two pizzas: one cut into 4 slices with 2 shaded, another cut into 8 slices with 4 shaded. Look! 2/4 and 4/8 show the same amount - they're equivalent fractions! Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number.

points.label: Equivalent Fractions
points.text: 2/4 = 4/8 = 1/2. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number.

slides.inSimpleWords: Same amount can be written as different fractions.

image.alt: Equivalent Fractions — Working with Fractions

slides.title: Simplifying Fractions
slides.storyContext: Arjun writes 6/9 and asks if he can simplify it. Priya nods: Find the GCD of 6 and 9. That's 3. Divide both by 3: 6÷3 = 2, 9÷3 = 3. So 6/9 = 2/3 in simplest form! A fraction is simplified when numerator and denominator share no common factors except 1.

points.label: Simplifying Fractions
points.text: Divide both numerator and denominator by their GCD. Keep dividing until no common factors remain.

slides.inSimpleWords: Make fractions smaller by dividing top and bottom.

slides.title: Worked Example: Simplifying
slides.storyContext: Let's practice simplification! Priya gives examples: 10/15 — GCD is 5, so divide both by 5 to get 2/3. 12/18 — GCD is 6, so divide both by 6 to get 2/3. Arjun tries: 9/12 — GCD is 3, so 9÷3 = 3, 12÷3 = 4. Answer: 3/4!

points.label: Quick Simplification Steps
points.text: 1. Find GCD of numerator and denominator. 2. Divide both by GCD. 3. Check if any factors remain.

slides.inSimpleWords: Keep dividing until you can't divide anymore.

slides.title: Improper Fractions and Mixed Numbers
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: What if the numerator is bigger than the denominator? Like 5/3? Priya explains: 5/3 means we have 5 thirds. That's 1 whole and 2/3 left over, or 1 2/3 as a mixed number. An improper fraction has a numerator ≥ denominator.

points.label: Improper Fractions
points.text: Numerator ≥ denominator. Example: 7/4. Can be written as mixed number: 1 3/4

slides.inSimpleWords: Improper fractions are bigger than or equal to 1.

slides.title: Converting Mixed Numbers to Improper Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches the reverse: To convert 2 3/5 to an improper fraction, multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and put it over the denominator. (2×5 + 3)/5 = 13/5. That's our improper fraction!
slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply whole by denominator, add numerator.

slides.title: Challenge: Mixed Fraction Arithmetic
slides.storyContext: Arjun adds: 2 1/4 + 1 2/4. Priya suggests two methods: (1) Convert to improper: 9/4 + 6/4 = 15/4 = 3 3/4. (2) Add whole parts and fractions separately: 2 + 1 = 3, 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4. Both work!

points.label: Adding Mixed Numbers
points.text: Add whole parts together. Add fractional parts together. Combine results. Simplify if needed.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add wholes, then fractions, then combine.

slides.title: Dividing Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya poses a puzzle: 1/2 ÷ 1/4 means how many 1/4s fit in 1/2? She draws a picture: four 1/4s fit in the whole, two fit in 1/2. So the answer is 2! Rule: To divide, multiply by the reciprocal. 1/2 × 4/1 = 4/2 = 2.

points.label: Dividing Fractions
points.text: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c). Flip the second fraction and multiply!

slides.inSimpleWords: Flip and multiply to divide fractions.

slides.title: Understanding Reciprocals
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns: A reciprocal is what you get by flipping a fraction. The reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2. The reciprocal of 5 is 1/5. When you multiply a fraction by its reciprocal, you always get 1! 2/3 × 3/2 = 6/6 = 1.

points.label: Reciprocals
points.text: Flip numerator and denominator. a/b × b/a = 1. Used in division.

slides.inSimpleWords: Flip fractions to get reciprocals.

slides.title: Challenge: Complex Fraction Problems
slides.storyContext: Priya challenges Arjun with a multi-step problem: (1/2 + 1/4) × 2/3. First, add: 1/2 = 2/4, so 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. Then multiply: 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2. Arjun solves it step by step!

points.label: Multi-Step Problems
points.text: Follow order of operations: parentheses first, then multiplication/division left to right.

slides.inSimpleWords: Solve step by step, one operation at a time.

slides.title: Fractions as Division
slides.storyContext: Priya connects a new idea: The fraction 3/4 actually means 3 ÷ 4. If you divide 3 by 4 on a calculator, you get 0.75! Every fraction can be turned into a decimal by dividing the numerator by the denominator.
slides.inSimpleWords: Divide the top by the bottom to get decimals.

slides.title: Real-World Fractions: Cooking with Recipes
slides.storyContext: At home, Arjun's mom uses fractions in recipes! A recipe calls for 1/2 cup sugar and 3/4 cup flour. Arjun doubles the recipe, so he needs 1 cup sugar and 1 1/2 cups flour. Fractions help us measure and scale real things in everyday life!

points.label: Practical Fractions
points.text: Cooking: measurements. Construction: dimensions. Shopping: discounts. Travel: distances. Fractions are everywhere!

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions help us measure real things.

slides.title: Challenge: Real-World Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya sets a challenge: A pizza restaurant sells 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 pizzas. Arjun's family wants 1 1/4 pizzas. What combination should they order? One option: 1/2 + 3/4 = 2/4 + 3/4 = 5/4 = 1 1/4. Perfect!

points.label: Problem-Solving
points.text: Identify what you know. Convert to same denominators. Add/subtract as needed. Check your answer.

example.problem: If 1/3 of a cake weighs 200g, how much does the whole cake weigh?

slides.inSimpleWords: Use fractions to solve everyday problems.

slides.title: Comparing and Ordering Fractions
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: To order fractions 3/8, 1/2, 5/12 from smallest to largest, find a common denominator. LCM(8,2,12) = 24. Convert: 3/8 = 9/24, 1/2 = 12/24, 5/12 = 10/24. Order: 9/24 < 10/24 < 12/24 or 3/8 < 5/12 < 1/2.

points.label: Ordering Fractions
points.text: Find common denominator. Convert all fractions. Compare numerators. Order by numerator size.

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert to same denominator, then compare tops.

slides.title: Worked Example: Complex Multi-Step Problem
slides.storyContext: Arjun solves: 1/2 of a pizza costs 200 rupees. What's the cost of 3/4 pizza? First, find full pizza cost: 200 × 2 = 400 rupees. Then 3/4 of 400 = 3/4 × 400 = 300 rupees. Fractions connect to real money!

points.label: Real-World Fraction Math
points.text: Identify what fraction you know. Find the whole. Calculate the unknown fraction.

example.problem: If 2/5 of a cake weighs 400g, what's the whole cake weight?

slides.inSimpleWords: Use fractions to solve word problems.

slides.title: Pizza Math Mastered
slides.storyContext: Walking home, Arjun and Priya review: Fractions have numerators and denominators. We add by finding common bottoms. We multiply by multiplying tops and bottoms. Equivalent fractions show the same parts differently. Arjun smiles. Now I can split anything fairly!

points.label: Fraction Mastery
points.text: Understand parts and wholes. Add with common denominators. Multiply numerators and denominators. Simplify to equivalent fractions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions are parts of wholes, shared and calculated.

image.alt: Pizza Math Mastered — Working with Fractions

subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun and Priya Discover Number Magic
hook: Explore factors, multiples, and prime numbers in this fun number adventure!

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: A number theorist revealing number secrets

slides.title: Arjun and Priya Discover Number Magic
What Divides Into 12?
slides.storyContext: At home, Arjun arranges 12 candies in rows. I can make 2 rows of 6, or 3 rows of 4, or 4 rows of 3! Priya nods. Those are factors of 12 - numbers that divide evenly into 12. Factors of 12 are: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12.
slides.inSimpleWords: Factors divide evenly into a number.

image.alt: What Divides Into 12? — Number Play

slides.title: Understanding Factors
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: A factor is a number that divides evenly into another number with no remainder. For 12, we can divide by 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, or 12 without remainder. These are all factors of 12!

points.label: Factors Defined
points.text: A factor of n is any number that divides n evenly (with remainder 0). Factors always come in pairs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factors divide into a number with no remainder.

slides.title: Prime and Composite Numbers
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Arjun cards with numbers: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Like 7 - only 1 and 7 divide into it! She shows another: 12 has many factors. It's composite. Arjun asks: Is 1 prime? Priya shakes her head. 1 is special - neither prime nor composite.

points.label: Prime vs. Composite
points.text: Prime: exactly 2 factors (1 and itself). Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. Composite: more than 2 factors. Example: 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prime numbers only divide by 1 and themselves.

image.alt: Prime and Composite Numbers — Number Play

slides.title: Identifying Prime Numbers
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya play a game: Is each number prime? 13: only 1 and 13 divide in — prime! 15: 1, 3, 5, 15 — composite! 2: only 1 and 2 — prime (and the only even prime!). 4: 1, 2, 4 — composite. Priya shows a list: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23 are all primes under 25.

points.label: Testing for Prime
points.text: Check if any number from 2 to √n divides n evenly. If none do, it's prime.

example.solution: Check 2, 3, 4. None divide 17 evenly. 17 is prime.

slides.inSimpleWords: Try to divide by small numbers. If none work, it's prime.

slides.title: Multiples — Skip Counting
slides.storyContext: Priya counts: Multiples of 3 are: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18... She hops on a number line. Each time, I skip by 3. These are all multiples of 3 - they all have 3 as a factor!

points.label: Multiples
points.text: Multiples of n: n×1, n×2, n×3... Example: multiples of 5 are 5, 10, 15, 20...

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiples are what you get by skip-counting.

image.alt: Multiples — Skip Counting — Number Play

slides.title: Finding Multiples Quickly
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants multiples of 6. Priya says: Just multiply 6 by 1, 2, 3, 4... 6×1=6, 6×2=12, 6×3=18, 6×4=24. Easy! Arjun tries multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45. Got it!

points.label: Generating Multiples
points.text: Multiply the number by 1, 2, 3, 4... as many times as needed.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiples = original number × 1, 2, 3, 4...

slides.title: GCD — Finding the Greatest Common Factor
slides.storyContext: Arjun has 12 marbles, Priya has 18. They want to divide them into equal piles with no leftovers. What's the largest pile size that works for both? asks Arjun. Priya lists: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The greatest common factor is 6! They make 2 piles of 6 marbles each.

points.label: GCD (Greatest Common Divisor)
points.text: The largest number that divides evenly into two numbers. GCD(12, 18) = 6

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD is the largest number dividing both.

image.alt: GCD — Finding the Greatest Common Factor — Number Play

slides.title: Methods to Find GCD
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches two ways: Method 1 — List all factors and find the biggest one in common. Method 2 — Prime factorization. For 12 and 18: 12 = 2² × 3, 18 = 2 × 3². Common factors are 2 and 3, so GCD = 2 × 3 = 6!

points.label: GCD Calculation
points.text: Prime factorization method: write as products of primes, multiply shared primes only.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find shared prime factors and multiply them.

slides.title: LCM — Finding the Least Common Multiple
slides.storyContext: Arjun's bus comes every 4 minutes. Priya's comes every 6 minutes. When will both buses arrive together? Priya calculates: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20... Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24... The least common multiple is 12. Both buses arrive together every 12 minutes!

points.label: LCM (Least Common Multiple)
points.text: The smallest number that is a multiple of both. LCM(4, 6) = 12

slides.inSimpleWords: LCM is the smallest number both divide into.

image.alt: LCM — Finding the Least Common Multiple — Number Play

slides.title: Calculating LCM with Prime Factorization
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: For LCM(12, 18), write prime factors: 12 = 2² × 3, 18 = 2 × 3². For LCM, take the HIGHEST power of each prime: 2² (from 12) and 3² (from 18). LCM = 2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36!

points.label: LCM Calculation
points.text: Prime factorization: take the highest power of each prime, multiply them together.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the highest powers of all primes.

slides.title: Challenge: GCD and LCM Together
slides.storyContext: Priya sets a challenge: For 20 and 30, find both GCD and LCM. 20 = 2² × 5, 30 = 2 × 3 × 5. GCD = 2 × 5 = 10. LCM = 2² × 3 × 5 = 60. Notice: GCD × LCM = 20 × 30 = 600!

points.label: GCD × LCM Formula
points.text: For any two numbers a and b: a × b = GCD(a,b) × LCM(a,b)

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD and LCM have a special relationship.

slides.title: Worked Example: Listing Common Multiples
slides.storyContext: Priya and Arjun list multiples side by side: Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36... Multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45... Common multiples are 18, 36, 54... The LEAST is 18! Arjun realizes: LCM is the first number that appears in both lists.

points.label: Finding LCM by Listing
points.text: Write multiples of each number. Find the smallest number that appears in both lists.

slides.inSimpleWords: List multiples until you find a match.

slides.title: Using Factor Trees for Prime Factorization
slides.storyContext: Priya draws a factor tree for 24: 24 splits into 8 and 3. 8 splits into 4 and 2. 4 splits into 2 and 2. The leaves are all primes: 2, 2, 2, 3. So 24 = 2³ × 3! Arjun loves the visual. Trees make factorization clear!

points.label: Factor Trees
points.text: Start with a number. Split into factors. Keep splitting until only primes remain. Read primes from leaves.

slides.inSimpleWords: Draw a tree to break numbers into primes.

slides.title: Worked Example: Drawing a Factor Tree
slides.storyContext: Let's draw a tree for 60! Priya and Arjun split it step by step: 60 → 6 and 10 → (2, 3) and (2, 5). The primes are 2, 2, 3, 5 on the leaves. So 60 = 2² × 3 × 5. Easy to visualize!

points.label: Factor Tree Steps
points.text: Write the number. Branch into any two factors. Keep branching until all leaves are prime. Multiply primes to verify.

slides.inSimpleWords: Branch until you reach prime numbers.

slides.title: Challenge: Complex GCD and LCM Problems
slides.storyContext: Priya challenges with two numbers: 84 and 126. Arjun finds: 84 = 2² × 3 × 7, 126 = 2 × 3² × 7. GCD = 2 × 3 × 7 = 42. LCM = 2² × 3² × 7 = 252. Verify: 84 × 126 = 10,584 and 42 × 252 = 10,584. Perfect!

points.label: Verification Using Formula
points.text: Always verify: a × b = GCD(a,b) × LCM(a,b). This confirms your calculations.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the formula to check if your GCD and LCM are correct.

slides.title: Divisibility Rules Make It Faster
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches shortcuts: A number is divisible by 2 if it's even. By 3 if its digit sum is divisible by 3. By 5 if it ends in 0 or 5. By 10 if it ends in 0. She checks 135: 1+3+5=9, which is divisible by 3, so 135 is too! Arjun tries 156: 1+5+6=12, divisible by 3! 156 ÷ 3 = 52!

points.label: Divisibility Shortcuts
points.text: Divisible by 2: even. By 3: digit sum is divisible by 3. By 5: ends in 0/5. By 10: ends in 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use shortcuts to check if numbers divide evenly.

image.alt: Divisibility Rules Make It Faster — Number Play

slides.title: More Divisibility Rules
slides.storyContext: Priya continues: Divisible by 4? Check if the last 2 digits form a number divisible by 4. By 6? Must be divisible by both 2 AND 3. By 9? Digit sum divisible by 9. By 11? Alternate digit sum divisible by 11. These save time without long division!

points.label: Advanced Divisibility
points.text: By 4: last 2 digits divisible by 4. By 6: divisible by 2 AND 3. By 9: digit sum divisible by 9. By 11: alternating digit sum.

slides.inSimpleWords: Learn patterns to test divisibility quickly.

slides.title: Prime Factorization
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: Can we break down any number into primes? Priya shows: 24 = 2 × 12 = 2 × 2 × 6 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2³ × 3. Every number has a unique prime factorization! She draws a factor tree showing how 24 breaks into its prime building blocks.

points.label: Prime Factorization
points.text: Every integer > 1 is either prime or a product of primes. This product is unique.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break numbers into their prime pieces.

slides.title: Perfect Numbers and Special Patterns
slides.storyContext: Priya discovers: 6 is special! Its factors are 1, 2, 3, and 1+2+3 = 6. It's a perfect number! Its factors (except itself) add to itself. 28 is the next one: 1+2+4+7+14 = 28. Arjun is amazed. Numbers have secret personalities!

points.label: Perfect Numbers
points.text: A perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors. Examples: 6, 28, 496.

slides.inSimpleWords: Perfect numbers equal their factor sums.

slides.title: Challenge: Real-World Number Problems
slides.storyContext: Priya challenges Arjun: A store has 36 apples and 48 oranges. They want to pack them into boxes with equal amounts of each fruit, no leftovers. What's the largest box size? GCD(36, 48) = 12. So 12 boxes with 3 apples and 4 oranges each!

points.label: Problem-Solving
points.text: Identify what you need (GCD for equal packing, LCM for timing). Find it. Apply to the problem.

example.problem: Lights blink: one every 6 sec, another every 9 sec. When do they blink together?

slides.inSimpleWords: Use factors and multiples to solve real problems.

slides.title: Worked Example: Real-World Problem with LCM
slides.storyContext: Arjun's school music class meets every 6 days. Drama club meets every 4 days. Both met today. When will they meet on the same day again? LCM(6, 4) = 12. In 12 days! Priya shows: multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18... multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12... Both hit 12!

points.label: LCM Application
points.text: When events repeat on different schedules, find LCM to know when they overlap.

example.problem: If one bell rings every 8 seconds and another every 12 seconds, when do they ring together?

slides.inSimpleWords: Use LCM to find when repeating events align.

slides.title: Odd and Even Numbers
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: Even numbers (divisible by 2): 2, 4, 6, 8, 10... Odd numbers (remainder 1 when divided by 2): 1, 3, 5, 7, 9... All primes except 2 are odd! Even + Even = Even. Odd + Odd = Even. Odd + Even = Odd.

points.label: Odd and Even Rules
points.text: Even: divisible by 2. Odd: remainder 1. Odd+Odd=Even. Even+Even=Even. Odd+Even=Odd.

slides.inSimpleWords: Odd numbers don't divide by 2. Even numbers do.

slides.title: Challenge: Twin Primes and Prime Patterns
slides.storyContext: Arjun discovers: Some primes are close together! 3 and 5, 5 and 7, 11 and 13, 17 and 19 are twin primes - they differ by 2. Priya explains: Nobody knows if twin primes go on forever! It's an unsolved math mystery. Every pattern has mysteries!

points.label: Twin Primes
points.text: Twin primes: two primes separated by 2. Examples: (3,5), (5,7), (11,13), (17,19), (29,31)...

slides.inSimpleWords: Twin primes are prime pairs 2 apart.

slides.title: Real-World Application: Packing Problem
slides.storyContext: A factory has 48 red balls and 36 blue balls. They want to pack them into identical boxes with no mixing, same amounts of each color per box, no leftovers. What's the largest box size? GCD(48, 36) = 12. So 12 boxes with 4 red and 3 blue balls each. Math solves real production problems!

points.label: GCD in Real Life
points.text: Finding equal-sized groups, fair distribution, resource allocation all use GCD.

example.problem: Pack 24 apples and 40 oranges into identical baskets. What's max basket size?
example.solution: GCD(24, 40) = 8. 8 baskets with 3 apples and 5 oranges each.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD solves packing and distribution problems.

slides.title: The World of Number Patterns
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya review their number adventure: factors, primes, composites, multiples, GCD, LCM. Numbers have hidden patterns! says Arjun. Priya smiles. Yes. And now you can see them all.

points.label: Number Fundamentals
points.text: Factors divide into numbers. Primes have 2 factors. Multiples are skip-counted. GCD and LCM solve shared problems.

slides.inSimpleWords: Number patterns connect factors, multiples, and primes.

image.alt: The World of Number Patterns — Number Play

subject: Science
title: Arjun and Priya's Garden Adventure
hook: Discover how plants make their own food in this green story!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: A curious gardener wondering how plants grow

slides.title: Why Do Plants Need Roots?
slides.storyContext: In their school garden, Arjun plants a seed. Priya says: The roots do two important jobs. First, they hold the plant in soil so it doesn't tip over. Second, they absorb water and minerals from the soil - that's nutrition! Arjun digs carefully. So roots are like a food pipeline?
slides.inSimpleWords: Roots absorb water and minerals for plant nutrition.

image.alt: Why Do Plants Need Roots? — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: The Root System
slides.storyContext: Priya explains roots in detail: Roots have a structure. The root cap protects the tip as it grows through soil. Root hairs are tiny threads that increase surface area for absorption. They absorb water and dissolved minerals like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium.

points.label: Root Structure
points.text: Root cap: protects growing tip. Root hairs: tiny extensions that absorb water and minerals. Xylem: tubes that carry water up.

slides.inSimpleWords: Roots have special parts to absorb and transport water.

slides.title: Green Power — Photosynthesis
slides.storyContext: Priya points at the green leaves. Inside these leaves, plants have a special power! They trap sunlight and use it to make food from water and air. It's called photosynthesis! She writes: Sunlight + Water + Carbon Dioxide = Glucose (sugar) + Oxygen.

points.label: Photosynthesis
points.text: Plants make glucose (food) using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. They release oxygen as a bonus!

example.problem: What three things does a plant need for photosynthesis?
example.solution: Sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide (from air)

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants make food using sun, water, and air.

image.alt: Green Power — Photosynthesis — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: The Photosynthesis Equation
slides.storyContext: Priya writes the equation carefully: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂. In words: 6 carbon dioxide molecules plus 6 water molecules plus light energy produces 1 glucose molecule and 6 oxygen molecules. Arjun realizes: Plants make oxygen for us to breathe!

points.label: Photosynthesis Formula
points.text: Carbon dioxide (from air) + Water (from roots) + Sunlight = Glucose (food) + Oxygen (for us)

slides.inSimpleWords: This equation shows how plants feed themselves and us.

slides.title: Chlorophyll — The Green Pigment
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: Why are leaves green? Priya smiles. Because of chlorophyll - a green pigment inside leaf cells. It captures sunlight! She holds up a leaf to the sun. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light, but reflects green light. That's why it looks green to us!

points.label: Chlorophyll
points.text: Green pigment in plant cells that captures sunlight for photosynthesis. It absorbs red/blue light and reflects green.

slides.inSimpleWords: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that traps sunlight.

image.alt: Chlorophyll — The Green Pigment — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Inside a Leaf: Stomata and Chloroplasts
slides.storyContext: Priya shows a microscope image: Inside leaves, there are tiny pores called stomata. They open to let carbon dioxide in and water vapor out. Inside cells, chloroplasts contain chlorophyll where photosynthesis happens! Arjun marvels. Leaves are like tiny factories!

points.label: Leaf Structure
points.text: Stomata: tiny pores for gas exchange. Chloroplasts: organelles containing chlorophyll where photosynthesis occurs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stomata let gases in and out. Chloroplasts make food.

slides.title: Heterotrophic Plants — Dodder and Mistletoe
slides.storyContext: Priya points at a vine wrapping around a tree. Not all plants are green! Some, like dodder, can't make their own food. They're parasites - they steal nutrients from other plants! Arjun shivers. That's mean! Priya nods. It's nature's strategy. Most plants are autotrophs and make their own food. A few are parasites.

points.label: Autotrophs vs. Parasites
points.text: Autotrophs (like most plants) make their own food. Parasites (like dodder) steal food from host plants.

slides.inSimpleWords: Most plants make food. Some steal it from other plants.

image.alt: Heterotrophic Plants — Dodder and Mistletoe — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Saprophytic Plants: Fungi and Decomposers
slides.storyContext: Arjun discovers mushrooms on a rotten log. Are these plants? Priya explains: Mushrooms are fungi, not plants. They're saprophytes - they break down dead material and absorb nutrients. They recycle nutrients back to soil! Without them, forests would be buried in dead leaves.

points.label: Saprophytes
points.text: Organisms that feed on dead or decaying matter. Examples: fungi, some bacteria. They decompose and recycle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Saprophytes break down dead things and feed soil.

slides.title: Minerals Plants Need
slides.storyContext: Priya shows a withered plant next to a healthy one. This plant had water but lacked nutrients. Plants need: nitrogen (for growth), phosphorus (for roots and flowers), potassium (for strength). She sprinkles fertilizer on the soil. Now it has all the minerals it needs!

points.label: Essential Minerals
points.text: Nitrogen: growth. Phosphorus: roots/flowers. Potassium: strength. Plants absorb these through roots.

example.problem: Why do farmers add fertilizer to soil?
example.solution: To provide nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium plants need for healthy growth

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants need minerals from soil for good health.

image.alt: Minerals Plants Need — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: The Role of Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Potassium
slides.storyContext: Priya details NPK (the main plant nutrients): Nitrogen builds proteins and green growth - that's why fertilizers boost leaf size. Phosphorus strengthens roots and helps flower/fruit development. Potassium regulates water and gives plants strength against stress. All three are essential!

points.label: NPK Functions
points.text: N: proteins, leaves. P: roots, flowers, seeds. K: water regulation, disease resistance.

slides.inSimpleWords: N for growth, P for roots/flowers, K for strength.

slides.title: Challenge: Nutrient Deficiency Symptoms
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns to diagnose problems: Yellow leaves? Nitrogen deficiency. Poor roots? Phosphorus deficiency. Weak stems? Potassium deficiency. By watching plants, we can tell what minerals they need! Priya shows examples of each problem.

points.label: Identifying Deficiencies
points.text: Yellow leaves = N. Weak roots = P. Weak stems = K. Purple leaves can mean P deficiency too.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plant symptoms show which nutrients are missing.

slides.title: Transpiration — Plants Release Water
slides.storyContext: Arjun covers a plant with a plastic bag. Within hours, water droplets appear inside. Where did that come from? he asks. Priya explains: Plants absorb more water than they use. They release extra water vapor through leaves - that's transpiration. The bag traps it, showing us!

points.label: Transpiration
points.text: Plants release water vapor through leaves. It's like plant sweating on a hot day.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants release water through leaves as vapor.

image.alt: Transpiration — Plants Release Water — Nutrition in Plants

slides.title: Water Transport: Xylem and Phloem
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches: Xylem vessels carry water and minerals UP from roots to leaves. Phloem tubes carry glucose DOWN from leaves to all plant parts. Together, they're the plant's transport system! Arjun imagines: Xylem is the input pipeline, phloem is the delivery system.

points.label: Transport Tissues
points.text: Xylem: water/minerals up. Phloem: glucose down. Both are vascular tissues.

slides.inSimpleWords: Xylem and phloem are plant plumbing systems.

slides.title: Observing Xylem Transport
slides.storyContext: Priya conducts an experiment: Cut a white flower stem and place it in water with red dye. Within hours, the petals show red streaks! The dye traveled through xylem vessels, proving water transport. Arjun does this with celery and sees red lines in the stem. Proof!

points.label: Experimental Evidence
points.text: Dye in water uptake shows xylem transport. Cut stem crosswise and you can see xylem as tiny dots.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dye experiments show how water moves through plants.

slides.title: Factors Affecting Photosynthesis
slides.storyContext: Arjun sets up an experiment: He puts one plant in bright sunlight, one in dim light, one in a sealed bag (no CO₂). Which grows best? The one with full sun and fresh air! Priya explains: Photosynthesis depends on light intensity, temperature, and CO₂ concentration.

points.label: Photosynthesis Factors
points.text: Light: more light = faster photosynthesis (up to saturation point). Temperature: 25-35°C optimal. CO₂: higher CO₂ = faster rate.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light, heat, and CO₂ all affect how fast plants make food.

slides.title: Respiration in Plants
slides.storyContext: Priya reveals a secret: Plants respire too! They use some glucose they make for their own energy. The equation is opposite to photosynthesis: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon Dioxide + Water + Energy. Arjun asks: So plants photosynthesize during the day and respire day and night?

points.label: Plant Respiration
points.text: Aerobic: glucose + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + energy. Occurs in mitochondria, day and night.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants breathe to use their own food for energy.

slides.title: Challenge: Net vs. Gross Production
slides.storyContext: Priya poses: A plant makes 100 units of glucose via photosynthesis, but uses 30 units for its own respiration. Net production = 70 units. That's what's available for growth and storage! Understanding this explains why some plants grow faster than others.

points.label: Gross vs. Net
points.text: Gross = total glucose made. Net = gross minus respiration. Net is what's left for growth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants make food but use some for their own energy.

slides.title: Nutrition in Different Plant Types
slides.storyContext: Arjun explores varieties: Most plants are autotrophs (make food). Carnivorous plants like Venus fly traps supplement with insect nutrients. Aquatic plants have no soil but absorb minerals from water. Arjun realizes: Every plant adapts to its environment!

points.label: Nutritional Adaptations
points.text: Autotrophs: most plants. Heterotrophs: parasites, saprophytes. Carnivorous: insects. Aquatic: from water.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different plants get nutrition in different ways.

slides.title: Worked Example: Calculate Net Production
slides.storyContext: Priya poses a calculation: A plant produces 500g of glucose but uses 200g for respiration. Net production = 500 - 200 = 300g. This 300g is available for storage in seeds and growth. Arjun now understands: Not all food stays in the plant!

points.label: Net Production Formula
points.text: Net = Gross production - Respiration loss. This is energy available for growth and storage.

example.problem: If a plant makes 100 units of glucose and uses 40 for respiration, what's net production?

slides.inSimpleWords: Subtract respiration from production to get net growth.

slides.title: Light-Dependent and Light-Independent Reactions
slides.storyContext: Priya teaches in detail: Photosynthesis has two stages. Light-dependent reactions (in thylakoids) capture sunlight and split water, releasing oxygen and energy. Light-independent reactions (in stroma) use that energy to build glucose from CO₂. Both are essential!

points.label: Two Stages of Photosynthesis
points.text: Light-dependent: needs light, produces ATP and O₂. Light-independent (Calvin cycle): builds glucose from CO₂.

slides.inSimpleWords: Photosynthesis has two parts: one needs light, one doesn't.

slides.title: Challenge: Compare Aquatic and Terrestrial Plants
slides.storyContext: Arjun wonders: Are aquatic plants different? Priya explains: Aquatic plants have no roots for anchoring (they float) and no xylem (water is everywhere). But they DO photosynthesize and absorb minerals. Desert plants have deep roots to find water. Every plant adapts!

points.label: Ecological Adaptations
points.text: Desert: deep roots, small leaves, thick waxy skin. Aquatic: no real roots, aerenchyma (air spaces). Rainforest: large leaves, thin waxy layer.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants change their structure based on their habitat.

slides.title: Worked Example: Measuring Transpiration
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya set up an experiment: weigh a plant with soil (500g). After 1 day in sunlight with no watering, it weighs 485g. The 15g loss is transpiration! Sunlight speeds transpiration. Temperature and humidity also matter. More sun = more water loss!

points.label: Transpiration Rate Factors
points.text: Sunlight: higher light = faster transpiration. Temperature: warmth speeds it. Humidity: drier air = faster loss. Wind: movement increases it.

example.problem: A plant loses 20g water in strong sunlight. In shade, only 5g. How many times faster?

slides.inSimpleWords: Measure transpiration by weighing the plant.

slides.title: Photosynthesis vs. Respiration: A Comparison
slides.storyContext: Priya creates a table: Photosynthesis (day) makes glucose + oxygen using sunlight. Respiration (all day) breaks down glucose to release energy. One builds food, the other uses it! Together they balance: photosynthesis feeds respiration; respiration fuels the plant's life.

points.label: Comparison Table
points.text: Photosynthesis: builds glucose, releases O₂, needs light. Respiration: breaks glucose, uses O₂, all-day process.

slides.inSimpleWords: Photosynthesis builds food. Respiration uses it.

slides.title: Challenge: Using Plants to Improve Air Quality
slides.storyContext: Priya and Arjun realize: Plants release oxygen during photosynthesis. That's why houseplants improve air quality! Spider plants, pothos, and peace lilies are popular air cleaners. The more active photosynthesis, the more oxygen! They resolve to add plants to every room.

points.label: Plants as Air Filters
points.text: Plants photosynthesize and release O₂. Many also absorb toxins (CO₂, formaldehyde). Natural air purifiers!

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants clean the air by making oxygen.

slides.title: Worked Example: Estimating Plant Oxygen Production
slides.storyContext: Priya calculates: During 8 hours of sunlight, a plant produces about 5 liters of oxygen. A person uses about 550 liters per day. You'd need about 110 plants to replace one person's oxygen! But plants also help by absorbing CO₂ we exhale.

points.label: Plant-Human Connection
points.text: Plants make O₂ for us. We make CO₂ for them. It's a perfect symbiosis!

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants and animals complete each other's cycles.

slides.title: The Complete Plant Story
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Priya sit under a mango tree. Roots absorb water and minerals. Leaves capture sunlight and make food. Plants release oxygen for us to breathe and water for the ecosystem. Everything is connected! says Priya. Arjun smiles. Plants are farmers of sunlight!

points.label: Plant Nutrition Summary
points.text: Roots absorb water/minerals. Photosynthesis makes food. Chlorophyll captures light. Plants are autotrophs except parasites.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants are self-feeding organisms using sun energy.

image.alt: The Complete Plant Story — Nutrition in Plants
